..
Issued at 337 AM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

Calm winds and mostly clear skies have allowed for fog to 
develop in portions of northern Illinois and northwest Indiana 
once again early this morning. Webcam observations suggest that 
a lot of this fog is shallow and patchy in coverage at this 
time, but a more expansive bank of thicker fog is evident on 
GOES Nighttime Microphysics and Fog imagery channels across
southeastern portions of our forecast area. This fog will 
continue to expand in coverage prior to sunrise, and 
visibilities of 1/4 mile or less should become more common with
time as well, so will be issuing a Dense Fog Advisory this 
morning for the affected areas.

After the fog burns off by the mid-late morning, today will
shape up to be another pleasant late September day with broad 
high pressure over the region. Yesterday, dew points mixed out 
fairly easily and air temperatures correspondingly overperformed
forecast guidance slightly in areas outside of Lake Michigan's 
influence. With the same air mass still in place over the region
today, would expect something similar to occur once again with 
temperatures climbing into the mid-upper 70s away from the 
lake's shadow, while temperatures in close proximity to the lake
struggle to climb above 70F. Another night of mostly clear 
skies and light/calm winds should then set the stage for another
round of fog potential in our forecast area tonight into 
Tuesday morning. Forecast guidance is particularly bullish on 
this fog developing within the footprint of the marine- 
influenced higher mixing ratio air that will have settled in 
over much of the Chicago metro and adjacent counties prior to 
sunset, so for starters, have added a patchy fog mention to the
forecast grids for these areas Tuesday morning. 

Longwave troughing over the western CONUS will facilitate the 
development of a frontal zone across the central CONUS by 
midweek. The slower eastward progression of this frontal zone 
that ensemble guidance has latched onto in the past day or two 
means that the same air mass will persist in our area through at
least Tuesday, and quite possibly through Wednesday as well. 
Tuesday should thus be another dry day here with slightly warmer
temperatures compared to today and yesterday. Should 
temperatures overperform raw model guidance once again (which 
currently seems more likely than not), then many of our southern
locales could climb into the low 80s Tuesday afternoon.

Temperatures on Wednesday will depend on how far east the 
aforementioned frontal zone and an associated corridor of 
expansive rainfall get. Southeastern portions of our forecast 
area will likely remain dry through the daytime on Wednesday and
should thus see another day of warm temperatures with highs in 
the upper 70s to the low-mid 80s. Meanwhile, ensemble guidance 
remains mixed on whether the rain shield will spread into the 
northwestern half or third of our forecast area. If the rain 
remains north and west of our area like the GEFS and GDPS are 
generally favoring, then mid-upper 70s highs should be 
attainable once again in our northwestern locales on Wednesday,
even with more extensive cloud cover. If a more 
southerly/easterly solution in line with most of the EPS's 
members were to verify and the rain (and possibly a few 
accompanying storms) were to spread into our northwestern 
counties during the daytime on Wednesday, then the mid 70s 
forecast high temperatures from the NBM for these areas are 
likely overdone, quite possibly by 10+ degrees.

Eventually, the frontal zone and the main axis of the 
associated rainfall will slide far enough eastward to engulf our
whole forecast area sometime on Thursday as an influx of 
combined Pacific and Gulf moisture is drawn northeastward into 
the Great Lakes region. How much rainfall we'll see and how 
quick the rain will be to skedaddle out of our forecast area 
remain points of considerable uncertainty with our forecast with
the various ensemble solutions still at odds on the extent to 
which the remnants of Pacific Hurricane Polo will phase with a 
cut-off upper low over the Desert Southwest. This is something 
that will need to be monitored closely, though, with good 
ensemble agreement on precipitable water values at least 
approaching, and possibly exceeding, 2" -- something that has 
only occurred a couple of times at the beginning of October in 
our neck of the woods since the mid 1990s, per sounding 
climatology at ILX and DVN. Either way, expect cooler 
temperatures to return for the end of the week into this coming 
weekend after the frontal zone has passed through the region.

Ogorek
